utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Two quick procedural matters more beyond procedure. We have all noticed the time it has taken to bring up the detailed map of Vukovar, Exhibit 59. The registry officer has been able to prepare from that Exhibit 59 a version which is less detailed in the intensity of the number of pixels. It, for most purposes, will do just as well as the more detailed map but will be able to be brought up on the screen in half the time. So could I invite all counsel, in future, unless there is some very special reason to go to the very detailed map, to use the other, which has been entered as an exhibit, I think 156. Exhibit 156 the less detailed map. The second matter is that the -- as counsel will be aware, on Monday we have a pre-programmed videolink for a witness who is unable to be here. For that reason, it would be highly desirable, if possible, for us to conclude this witness today, because we must go to the videolink on Monday. So I would ask all counsel to bear that in mind. If I could remind you, sir, of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies. Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday you talked about leaving the Vukovar Hospital and leaving on a bus with a group of other buses and arriving at the JNA barracks on the 20th of November, 1991. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you also said that when you arrived at the JNA barracks the buses parked in a semicircle inside the barracks, and then there was a number of paramilitaries that were surrounding the buses and threatening the people in the buses, including yourself. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Just so give the Court a bit more understanding of what the atmosphere was like and what these men were doing, can you describe in a bit more detail as to what they were doing whilst you were sitting on the bus in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They surrounded the buses. Most of those were local Serbs, local Serb paramilitaries, threatening us with knives and rifles saying that they would slit our throats and kill us. There was this one man, an acquaintance of mine, they threatened him that they would rape his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if you could name that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mihovil Zero.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how long did this threatening go on for? How long were they surrounding the buses and carrying on in this manner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 10 and 15 minutes, I reckon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how were you feeling at that stage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an awful feeling. At least the feeling I had was awful, having realised that this was not the way I thought it would be. This was no interview or questioning. The way matters looked at this point, I thought the worst would happen to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said this surrounding and threatening by these people were -- was carrying on for about 10 to 15 minutes. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that a military officer got onto the bus, some sort of a commander. That's what I thought at least. He obviously had quite some authority over the others because everything suddenly got very quiet. He went from bus to bus, asking everybody if we knew the whereabouts of Sinisa Glavasevic, Josip Esterajher, Dr. Zlatko Simunovic, Dr. Farkas, Dr. Emedi, and Dr. Sijanovic. When we told him that we had no idea, he started calling out names of individuals - he called out my name too - and told us to go to another bus that was waiting there empty at a distance of perhaps 30 metres from the other buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. You gave a number of names that he was looking for or calling out and you gave them quite fast, so perhaps if we just go back a minute. And if we can talk about the military officer that got on the bus that you said seemed to have some sort of command or authority over the -- over the men outside of the bus. What sort of military group did he belong to when you say he was a military officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He belonged to the JNA. He was wearing the JNA uniform head to toe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how was his appearance compared to the appearance of the other men that were surrounding the buses? Was there any difference?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference was ineffable. He was very orderly, clean-shaven, with a recent haircut. Everything was spick and span, as people say, including his uniform. A proper soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And again, you said that he came onto the bus, and he called out some names initially. And I'm just wondering if you could go through those names a lot more slowly than you did before so that we can record it on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simunovic, Dr. Zlatko; Emedi, Dr. Vladimir; Farkas, Dr. Ladislav; Sinisa Glavasevic; Josip Esterajher; and Sijanovic, Dr. Andrija.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, what ethnicity were these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people were ethnic Croats with the exception of Dr. Farkas, who was a Hungarian. And Dr. Emedi was a Ruthenian by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were any of those people on the bus that you were on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you see any of those people whilst you were at the JNA barracks on other buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then after this, did this JNA officer, did he leave the bus, or stay on the bus after he was looking for these people.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He left the bus, and I imagine he went to the other buses to announce the same thing and ask the same question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you know these people and did you know where they worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, are you referring to the people I have just described, the doctors that they were looking for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew them all quite well, all the doctors, and Sinisa Glavasevic, I did not know Josip Esterajher though.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said that after he entered your bus he went to other buses apparently looking for these people. Whilst he was going to the other buses, what was the situation with the paramilitaries you mentioned outside of the buses that had surrounded them? You said that quietened down. Was that the same situation, or had things changed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation had already quietened down, but this high-ranking officers who called out our names told us to go to the other bus that was parked about 30 metres away from the remaining buses. The paramilitaries then formed a gauntlet, and as we passed through it they kicked us with their boots, with clubs and with iron rods. Whichever way they could. We ran over to the other bus, because we knew that if any of us fell to the ground they would probably beat us to death.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And just so it's clear, you said that the JNA officer came on to your bus and was looking for that -- that group of doctors that you -- that you have mentioned. And then you said that he went to the other buses. Did he then come back to your bus or what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw him again, but there is one correction I have to make. Not all of them were doctors. Two of them were journalists. Josip Esterajher and Sinisa Glavasevic. The rest of them were doctors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when the JNA officer was looking for this group, did he also call out your name, or was that on a second occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this was a capricious and leading question. The next time the officer did not call out the witness's name because we just heard the witness stating "I never saw the officer again," so it wasn't possible for him to see the officer again or for the officer to call out his name. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think earlier in the transcript that the witness stated that he was called out, I believe. Right at the very beginning. I was seeking to clarify whether, in fact, the officer had come back on a second occasion, but I can clarify it with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's your reference to the second occasion that I think with some justification has concerned Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll approach it another way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, how many times did that JNA officer come on to the bus that you were on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: After the JNA officer came on to the bus did you get off the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Only those whose names had been called out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was your name called out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you remember the -- any other people from your bus whose names were called out that got off the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only one I remember is Rudolf Wilhelm, and Kolja Kolesar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said your names were called out, so you got off the bus. What were you told to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told to go to that empty bus that was parked about 30 metres away from the remaining buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who told you to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That military officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you got off the bus, can you explain more fully what happened to you specifically?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically this wasn't just me. This applied to all the others who were on their way. The paramilitaries had formed a gauntlet through which we had to pass on our way to that bus. They hit us and kicked us using all sorts of implements. Iron rods, wooden clubs, kicked us with their boots, with their rifle-butts. They used whatever they could lay their hands on to hit us with until we eventually reached the other bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said earlier that there were about 100 or so paramilitaries. Were they all involved in the gauntlet or was it only some of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them, not all of them. At least to the extent that I was able to observe and to the extent that I am now able to remember, 15 years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what happened to you exactly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was beaten just like those who had gone before me. I tried to protect myself because I was carrying my suitcases which I used to shelter from the blows. But on the other side, the side of my body where I wasn't carrying my suitcase, they were hitting me, using all sorts of different implements and whatever they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what about people from the other buses? Were people coming from the other buses and running through this gauntlet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we all met the same fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after running through these paramilitaries or through the line, did you eventually get on to the other bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we did. But that other bus was just as dreadful. There were two paramilitaries who were mistreating me specifically. There was a blond paramilitary who hit me twice. And the other man, the notorious Milan Bulic, who used to work as a butcher in the kitchen was beating all the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you mentioned that you and others went from one bus to the other one through this gauntlet of paramilitaries, about how long did that take in minutes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't catch the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The beating that was happening to yourself and the others that came off the other buses, for about how long did that take whilst you were outside of the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it went on until we reached that new bus, but it continued on that bus too, because there were two persons on that bus who continued to beat us. Milan Bulic, also known as Bulidza, and I didn't really know the other person's place. He was from one of the villages in the surroundings of Vukovar. I was told this later on by people who had, in fact, recognised him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how many people were put on to that other bus in addition to yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 30, 40 perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And whilst you were being beaten and the others were being beaten outside of the buses, did anyone attempt to stop this from continuing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No one attempted to stop this from happening. The few proper regular JNA officers who were there saw this going on but they just did nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you see what the JNA officer was doing whilst you were being beaten? And I'm referring to the one that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is tantamount to leading the witness. First of all, we should ascertain whether there was a JNA office present at the scene at this point in time. Only after that has been ascertained can we have a question like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, that was established by the previous question -- or the previous answer. Yes. You're quite right, but it actually had been established.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. Indeed. You're right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Still, I have to justify my objection. I was listening to the B/C/S interpretation. The witness said the few JNA soldiers who were outside did nothing about that. Can we please clarify this with the witness, because that's what I understand the witness to have said. The few soldiers who were outside the bus failed to react, or something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not outside the bus but, rather, around the bus and around that gauntlet there. There were soldiers there, but there was no reaction from them to what those other people were doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Once you were called off the bus, off the first bus, and before you ran through the gauntlet, how long did it take you to get off the bus after your name was called?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five minutes is what it took us to reach the empty bus, which we then got on to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you know what the JNA officer was doing, the one that called you off the bus whilst you were being beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. Your Honour, it is not my intention to be interrupting my learned friend all the time but we can go back to the transcript where the witness said, I did not see this officer again, the officer who I believe went to the other bus, which I believe renders this question superfluous. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Possibly superfluous, but it's perhaps desirable to get clear. And so the question asked is: Do you know what the JNA officer was doing, the one that called you off the bus? What was he doing whilst you were being beaten? Could you help us with that, please, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, of course. I suppose that he went to the remaining four or five buses. I suppose he went there. And as everybody was leaving, I imagine he must have been watching this and he must have seen what was happening and that we were being mistreated and yet he did nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You say you imagine. Did you actually see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't actually see him. I may even have seen him, to be quite frank, but the fear was so great and the pressure was so great that we only realised once we had reached the barracks what was going on at all. The fear was so great that under all the pressure and fear, you failed to realise clearly what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, now that you had run through the gauntlet and got on to the other bus where you say there were 30 other people on it, you mentioned that the beatings continued. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you mentioned that Milan Bulic and another person with blond hair was -- were executing carrying out the beatings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Both of them belonged to the paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And apart from the people that were called out and told to go to this other bus, including yourself, was there anyone else on that bus in addition to these two paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was nobody else on that bus except for the driver of the bus. That is, two paramilitaries, and another JNA soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you say there was another JNA soldier on the bus, are you saying that the driver was a JNA soldier or are you saying that there was a driver and a JNA soldier on the bus? Can you clarify that for us? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the driver and another JNA soldier who was standing at the entrance to the bus. He was there for our protection, so to say, but as far as I could see this was a young man recruit who may have been recruited a day or two prior to the events. He was a child.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why do you believe he may have been recruited a day or two before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we were being abused in the other bus he was astonished and afraid. One could see that clearly. He was clearly a child still.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the driver of this bus, were you able to ascertain whether he was a civilian or a military driver?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military driver. He wore a helmet and a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And from which military group did he belong?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He belonged to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was -- you mentioned that people were being beaten on this bus. Is there anyone in particular or any people in particular that you remember were being beaten - and take your time - on this bus.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember very well. I remember Milan Bulic, I used to know him very well, as he used to work in our -- in the kitchen of the hospital before the war. First he used an iron bar to hit Jozo Zeljko. He hit him on the neck and on the head. And with his military boot he kicked him in the face. He fell to the ground in blood, and he asked Milan, "How many lunches and dinners did you have at my place," because before the war they used to be friends. Jozo Zeljko's wife and Milan Bulic used to work in that kitchen together. And Milan Bulic's response to that was that he turned to the JNA conscript, saying, "Give me your rifle to kill him so that I can have some Croatian blood."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what did the JNA conscript do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. He didn't give him his rifle, but he remained silent and afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you explain to the Court if Jozo was a short name for something for -- for another name or is that a full -- a full name, full first name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was his full name, Jozo Zeljko.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how old was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time he may have been 35 to 40. Since I was 50 at the time, he was my junior by some 10 years, so he was probably around 35 or 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And is Jozo ever used as a short name for Josip in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. But I don't know whether his name was actually Josip. We all knew him as Jozo. I don't know anything else, whether he was Jozo or Josip. But it is correct that in Croatia one can have a -- the name of Josip but he can be known as Jozo, but in this case I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after you got on the bus with the other 30 or so, how long did you stay at the JNA barracks before you left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were you told at all where you were being -- where you were going to be taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Bulic, or that is Milan Bulic, aka Bulidza, told us we were being taken before the firing squad.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did he say where that firing squad was going to be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't say anything apart from that, that we were being taken to -- before the firing squad.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court where you were taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took us in front of the hospital, that's where we were loaded on to the buses initially and then we were returned there. But not to the main gate, but rather to the side entrance which is call Sapudle at the Gunduliceva Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was the driver, the other JNA soldier, and those two other paramilitaries, were they still on the bus when you arrived back at the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The two paramilitaries were there, and the driver. They all came to the side or back entrance of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And once you got back to the hospital, did they tell you to stay, did they tell you to leave? What did they tell you to do, if anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't tell us anything. But in the meantime, spouses of some men appeared, because most of the men were husbands to nurses or physicians at the hospital, and they had probably gone to Major Sljivancanin who approved that they could go out. They managed to explain to him that those were people who didn't carry arms, who used to work on odd jobs at the hospital or help out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were you able to get off that bus? And if you were, can you explain how that occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I managed to get off, but I was one of the last, and at the last moment I noticed a Serb colleague, a woman, who was the head of the hospital pharmacy. I knocked on the window, she saw me, and she went to see Mr. Sljivancanin, and she managed to get me out as well as my brother and my nephew. Behind me, as far as I can remember, there remained Miroslav Vlaho, Mato Vlaho, Jozo Adzaga, Jozo Zeljko, and another person whose name I don't know. I do know that he worked at Jugopetrol. He was abused and mistreated because they claimed he killed a prominent Serb in Vukovar known as Jovo Rakijica. At the time they were getting off the bus, Zeljko, Jozo and Adzaga, Jozo asked me in tears to go see the head of the kitchen, Mrs. Anica, to go and see Mr. Sljivancanin and to pray for their release, and to tell Mr. Sljivancanin that they carried no arms but that they had cooking jobs in the hospital kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court of the name of the woman that assisted you in getting off the bus? You say she went to speak to Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Her name was Gordana Bosnic. During the war, close to the end of the war, she was the head of the hospital pharmacy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how did you know that she had to get and others had to get Mr. Sljivancanin's approval for you to get off the bus? How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I knocked on her window, she explained that she would go and see Major Sljivancanin to ask for our release. That's how I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then once you were released, did you discover if there was any involvement of Mr. Sljivancanin, in fact? That's what she said was going to happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your apologies, but could you repeat the question? I didn't comprehend completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: She said Ms. Bosnic said to you that she would seek Mr. Sljivancanin's approval for you to get off the bus. Is that why you believe he was involved in that, or did you discover later more information to know that that was, in fact, the case or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got that piece of information right away, because we all knew who was the main person there. And he was the one to say who could leave the -- the hospital compound and who could get off the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And just to be clear, how did you know that he was the main person there that would provide that approval?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were brought in front of the hospital on the buses he was there. And he was present as the first few people got off the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So are you saying that he was present when you first left the Vukovar Hospital and you saw him again when you arrived back after the JNA barracks? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness replied that he saw Sljivancanin when they returned to the hospital, and then the Prosecutor, posing his next question, suggested to the witness that he was also present as they were leaving the Vukovar Hospital. And that's not what the witness was saying in the first part of his testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that the Prosecutor had in mind the following, that is, when we were leaving on the convoy, when we were leaving the hospital, that's when Major Sljivancanin was present. I suppose that's what the Prosecutor had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, Mr. Lukic's objection is well-founded. There has been no indication of that in the evidence so far. If you could be more careful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Just with respect, Your Honour, if I look at the answer at line 15 on page 16, the witness said: "When we were brought in front of the hospital in the buses he" - and obviously "was" is missed out - "there and he was present as the first few people got off the buses." And so that's why the question was based, because when he came back he was only on the one bus, but he was talking about -- it seemed to refer to when he left --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That answer you have referred to is speaking only about the return of the one bus to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, but it seems as though --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You have introduced the departure earlier to go away from the hospital. And that's the point of concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I mean, I accept your ruling, Your Honour, but it seems that he introduced some information that applied to that earlier situation, which obviously wasn't said yesterday. But I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Neither Mr. Lukic nor I think that the witness introduced it. We think you introduced it. The witness has confirmed it. It is now his evidence, but it was at your prompting. Thank you, Mr. Smith. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you got off the bus, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got off the bus I went straight to the then head of the military kitchen, because during the war that was the military hospital and the military kitchen. I went to tell her that I was asked by Zeljko and Adzaga Jozo to go to see Mr. Sljivancanin and ask for their release since they carried no weapons and that he was to tell him that they were only performing their duties in the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you go to Mr. Sljivancanin, or what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go to see Mr. Sljivancanin. I asked Anica Sila to do that. She was the head of the hospital kitchen. I was asked by the two colleagues who remained on the bus that I go and see her so that she could go and talk to Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you see her, and what did she do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see what she did. I did see her leave, though, with the intention to go and look for Mr. Sljivancanin on -- in the compound of the hospital. She went to see him, she explained the situation, and Mr. Sljivancanin told her, "Wait a few moments and we'll deal with it." But one of the paramilitaries later on whispered something to him on the side, and after that he told Anica Sila the following: "You may go now. If they are innocent, they will be released. If they're guilty, they will remain." And unfortunately, so it was, and they ended up at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who told you that Mr. Sljivancanin said this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the kitchen, Ms. Anica Sila.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many people were left on the bus after -- after you got off?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I got off, some seven people remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you see the bus leave, or did it stay there before you -- did it stay there before you left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was still there, but I don't know for how long. As Ms. Sila Anica was still with Mr. Sljivancanin, the bus was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you leave the Vukovar Hospital that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day, what do you mean if I left? It is unclear. Because for a while I was at the barracks, and when I returned and released, I left on the convoy. I don't know what exactly you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how long after you were released did you go on the convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five to 10 minutes at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say it was a convoy, what type of vehicles were in that convoy and about how many people were on it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be specific as to the number of the vehicles. It seemed to me around 10 buses; there may have been more or less. And the people on them were the medical personnel, physicians, nurses, and the technical staff. Apart from that, in the military medical vehicles, there were those people from the hospital in Vukovar who were gravely injured or wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how many medical vehicles were on this convoy, approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were at least 10 medical vehicles, because there were a lot of those who were seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And where were you told -- or were you told where you were going to go from there, and where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told that we were to leave to Croatia, but we were then driving towards Nustar, which was the way towards Croatia, but rather towards Serbia [as interpreted]. They kept saying that they were negotiating with Tudjman and that Tudjman wouldn't have us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And on the way, what route did you take and what places did you pass or stop at, of significance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time we stopped after leaving the hospital was at Velepromet. Even to this day it remains unclear to me. We saw two of our employees there, one of whom left in June before the war, an orthopaedist, Dr. Maric, and we knew he was in Negoslavci. And the other person was -- his last name was Arsenic; I can't remember his first name. Yes, it is Zeljko, Zeljko Arsenic. And he remained there until the very last moment. He was taking down those seriously wounded and then he went to Velepromet to wait for us in his military uniform. Zeljko Arsenic was an anaesthesologist with the hospital throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what type of military uniform was it? Could you work out the group to which he was belonging to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm with any degree of certainty whether it was a paramilitary uniform or not. Dr. Maric was the only one in full uniform. Zeljko Arsenic was carrying something of military nature, but I'm not sure whether it was an entire uniform. It's been 15 years. I can't recall exactly, but I think he was wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you stopped at Velepromet, did you park outside the location, or did you go inside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We parked in front to -- of the main gate of Velepromet. We didn't go in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how long did you park out the front of Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after that I believe you stayed the night at Sremska Mitrovica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. We came to Sremska Mitrovica, and as we parked to our left there was a large building with our men and women from Vukovar. They were detained there. On the other side there was a military facility, and when we got off the buses, we were received quite well. They gave us warm tea and food as well as a blanket each. And having eaten, we returned to the buses, and until next morning nobody moved from the buses. The people from the international community who were in our escort recommended that we do not leave the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said it was a military facility. Belonging to which military group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then the next day you travelled further on. Is that correct? And where did you end up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next day -- or, rather, the next morning we drove through Bosnia and reached Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Witness, I'm going to ask you some further questions about some of the people that you believe -- may believe are missing from those buses that you were on, on the 20th of November. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Zero, he was on my bus, Mihovil Zero.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I can just interrupt for a moment. I'm just going to go through it step by step, and if you could just listen to the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that at this point we go into private session. The witness is familiar with a number of these people, and I think that might lead to identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I will call for one last exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in public session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You would like to tender this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I would like to tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Under seal, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Received under seal under reference 159, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If we can call document number 65 ter, 224, it's a booklet of 11 photographs of the Vukovar Hospital. I would ask that the photograph 00531257A be called up. I think that is the last photograph of the group, if we could go to the first one which is 1257A. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, do you see the photograph on the screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court what that's a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a photograph of the hospital and the hospital surroundings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, Witness, in your evidence you talked about the kitchen where you worked, the old hospital building. Can you just point with an arrow where that old hospital building is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you mark that with an A, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Also, could you mark on that photograph the location where you left, you finally left the Vukovar Hospital to go to Croatia when you came back on the 20th of November? And if you could mark that with a B, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That marking, just for the record, looks like a 13, so that can do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've given it my best shot. This is how it comes out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Very nicely. Thank you. If we can --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll have another go. No, I can't. It's worse now, if anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I think we all understand. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I seek to tender that photograph, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. I have no objection to this, but one thing I'm not clear about is this marking, the letter A. Is that in reference to the other building, with the ground floor, or is it in reference to a building that can't be seen in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's in reference to another building which is not in the photograph, which is about 50 metres away from the main building.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this clarification. I think my learned friend had better find a photograph where we can see that building actually. I think that's probably more use than this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will received under the reference 160, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. We will get to that photograph. If we can move to 00531258.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, on the photograph that's in front of you could you mark the location where the buses left to go to Croatia and mark that with an A, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That marking that you just put, is that the location from where the buses left? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was right here. But this continues further down and to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the name of the street that the buses were parked on, the ones that left to go to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivo Lola Ribar Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you also mark with a B the emergency entrance to the hospital, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you mark with a C the location from where you were taken to the JNA barracks on those buses.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you also draw a line which would represent the underground corridor you referred to in your evidence that joined the old hospital to the new hospital, approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if you can mark that with a D, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender that photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be exhibit number 161.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And I'll now have a photograph that Mr. Vasic will like. 00531259, please. Your Honour, I think this process will take about probably five minutes, as I go through the photographs, then I will be finished with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, you should have the photograph in front of you now. Could you mark with an A the new hospital building, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you could mark with a B the old hospital building, where the kitchen was located. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you could mark with a C the exit that you came out of when you left the Vukovar Hospital for the first time at the end of the underground corridor.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you mark that exit with a C, please? The beginning of that line.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you indicate, perhaps with some crosses, the location where the JNA soldiers were that had lined up and were searching you and others as you were leaving the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if we can have Exhibit 00531260, please. I seek to tender that photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be exhibit number 162.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, on this photograph can you draw again the line from the exit, which you took from the main hospital building to the buses when you first went to the JNA barracks, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And perhaps if you could put an arrow on the end to show the direction that you took.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Again, could you mark some Xs as to where the JNA soldiers were as you were being searched when you left.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I seek to tender that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be received under reference 163, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just in order to dispel any doubts, in the previous photograph I think the witness marked the soldiers in one line, whereas -- or it might be my mistake, Your Honour, actually. It's my mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We can do two or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If we can have 00531262.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell the Court what this is a picture of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this photograph you can see the underground corridor connecting the new building and the old building. This is the entrance to the old building, and the makeshift kitchen was just around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If you could mark that with an A, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be received under the reference 164, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I can call 00531263 -- sorry, I'll slow down. Your Honour, I think I was being a little optimistic with the time that the photos take to come up on the screen, so maybe it would be a good time to break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the first -- there it is. Deal with that one, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell the Court what this is a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this photograph you can see the exit to the new building, the new hospital. The new hospital building. And to the left you can see the entrance to the nuclear shelter, which had two small rooms in it. That was a proper nuclear shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you can mark the entrance to that nuclear shelter with an A, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And perhaps if you can draw an arrow to the actual entrance itself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]

utterances.text: Witness, if you look at the photograph that will be put on the screen, it's the ERN number 00531264. Witness, in that photograph there are three doorways. Do you recognise what they are the doorways to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise them, and I will point at them with the marker. This here was the Crisis Staff, this is where Mrs. Vesna Bosanac sat. This is the plaster room where Mr. Sljivancanin had his speech delivered to the medical staff, and this is the emergency exit. In the extension there are two surgical rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Could you mark the entrance to the Crisis Staff room with the letter A, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you can mark the plaster room with the letter B, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if you can mark the emergency exit with the letter C, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if you can mark the extension where there were two surgical rooms with the letter D, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And, Witness, is the emergency exit to the hospital the same as the emergency entrance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It is the same thing. Excuse me, I didn't understand, at least I'm not quite certain. Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You marked the emergency exit with the letter C. And I'm asking whether that is the same as the emergency entrance into which the ambulances come in with the emergency patients?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ambulances didn't come in, but they stopped in front of the door. As I said, there is a hallway at the back of the picture, and as we could see in some of the previous pictures, there were benches in that corridor, or rather, stretchers on wheels to receive such patients. And behind that is where the ambulances were parked. Here, further down, is the corridor, and only then the exit from the emergency ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you mark that with an E, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honours. I seek to tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be received under the reference 166, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I could ask for Exhibit 00531265. That's the following photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It is what I was trying to explain a minute ago. That's the extension of the corridor, and the stretchers with wheels, and there is another stretcher in front of the door as the emergency exit was protected by planks. This is where patients were received and then taken on to the surgery or some other place in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you mark the doorway with the letter A, where the patients came in? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I seek to tender that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Under reference 167, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I could ask that the following photograph be called up, ending in 1266, 00531266.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And, Witness, do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, this is the emergency entrance. As I said, this is where the ambulances would park, bringing patients in and then one would go through here towards the surgery. And this is exactly where we went out when we were taken to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you mark the photo with the letter A, the doorway which is the emergency exit or entrance.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you can mark with an arrow, pointing the direction that you took when you left to go to the JNA barracks on the 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you mark again with Xs the approximate locations of the JNA soldiers that were searching you and your colleagues as you were leaving the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I seek to tender that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: With the reference 168, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if I can call the last photograph, 00531267. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That's the exit, or rather not the main entrance, but the side-gate from the Sapudle Street, or Gunduliceva Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you draw an arrow from the street to the location of the emergency entrance or exit, as you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I seek to tender that photograph, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be received under the reference 169, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek also to tender the full photographic book, which contains 11 photographs, unmarked, of what the witness has just been looking at, that were taken in 1997 under the direction of investigator in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You tender it as a booklet or in electronic form.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In electronic form. Thank you, Your Honour. That's 65 ter number 224.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Under reference 170, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, just a couple of last questions from me. Do you know a person by the name of Zvonko Varenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zvonko Varenica, I do know him. He's our plumber.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When was the last time that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last time I saw him was when he was with me on the bus at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: On the bus, as you were leaving the barracks -- sorry, I'll rephrase that question. When you left the barracks, was he on the bus with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we left the barracks he remained behind on one of the buses that we were called out from. Or, rather, the one that we were called out from.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how old was Zvonko in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was between 30 and 35. I am not certain. He had two children who were still of elementary school age.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And have you heard of him being alive since that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, unfortunately. I attended his funeral because he was one of those identified at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, this person also appears in the annex to the indictment. And I've completed my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Having in mind your instructions and our wish to meet the needs of the witness, because we were told that the witness would soon have to leave due to his obligations, and having in mind that the examination-in-chief lasted one hour 45 minutes instead of 45 minutes, but we will try to do our utmost, although I cannot promise that we will meet the dead-line set by ourselves and that we had in mind before the examination-in-chief finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I thank you for that, Mr. Vasic. If attention it focused on those parts of the witness's evidence that really matter, they're clear, a lot of it is just side material, I think you might be able to accomplish it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, I would like to introduce myself. I'm Miroslav Vasic, counsel for Mr. Mrksic. Since we speak a language that we both understand, could you please make pause between question and answer so that we would give time to the interpreters? There is another point to it; that is, you should give time to me to turn my microphone off as you are a protected witness, so that your voice would not leave the courtroom. On the 16th of July, 1995 you provided a statement to the representatives of the OTP, and it was read out to you in your mother tongue. You signed the statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What you mentioned in the statement was the best you could recollect at the time, although it was four years later, that is, four years after the events. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You also testified before this Tribunal in a case in February of 1998. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And at that time you also testified as best you could in terms of your memory. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You also participated in the proceedings initiated by the Croatian authorities -- or, rather, in the process of gathering information on the missing persons, and you also provided some information. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question? I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I will repeat. Having arrived to Croatia, you provided information to the Croatian authorities pertaining to those missing from Vukovar, and you participated in the process of creation of that list of the missing persons. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I collected such data as I was under a work obligation, I worked for the Croatian Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please do not provide us with unnecessary data because you could give your identity away.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In addition to that, did you also speak with some representatives of international organisations dealing with the protection of human rights and did you provide any sort of statement to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never discussed such matters with any of such representatives and I never provided any statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The institution you were employed with in Vukovar, its staff was of various nationalities. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In your work-place as well as in the part of the city where you lived you associated with members of all the nationalities represented in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In December of 1992 [as interpreted] and January 1991, did any of your Serb friends tell you that they felt endangered or deprived of their rights when the new Croatian constitution was put into force declaring Serbs as a national minority?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs did not mention that they felt deprived or anything of such nature. I never heard that from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: A correction for the transcript, page 43, line 6, December 1991 -- no, 1990 instead of 1992. In spring of 1991, were there unarmed units organised in Vukovar composed of members of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't respond to that since I was never -- never busied myself with politics, and it is a purely political question unrelated to the topic of our discussion today.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I just asked you if you were familiar with such a fact; my intention was not a political one.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I never busied myself with politics. I did not even vote at the elections. I simply dislike politics. I did not vote for Tudjman or anyone else. I simply did not vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now go to the 2nd of May, 1991. That is, I presume, the day you will never forget.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will never forget that day, because I was sitting in my office and I received a call that I should put all the ambulances and other available vehicles to the disposal and to be sent to Borovo Selo because a massacre took place. I also wanted to go, but my colleagues, drivers, told me that I should be at the gate to help them out because there were numerous vehicles concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you with a view of the fact that we need to complete this cross-examination as soon as possible and you need to leave to keep your answers brief, so that we could move quickly. That day you suffered shock and you were subsequently treated for it, and you lost 20 kilos in weight.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You were in shock because you were present when Serb citizens from Borovo Selo were brought into the hospital. They were injured with fragmentation bullets. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When did you return to work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In August.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The situation in hospital had already been changed by then. Were new measures introduced by the Ministry of Health creating the Crisis Staff and the necessary pre-conditions to receive those wounded and injured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were in place already.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The ethnic make-up of those employed at the hospital, has that changed? Did some Serbs, nurses and doctors, have left by that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as well as some others, some cooks, some drivers, a few nurses and doctors. They had left the hospital by the time I returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was another hospital manager appointed by the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The replacement was made prior to August. Much earlier, I believe, in June or July, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac headed the staff in the hospital until the 21st of November, 1991. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, the question concerned Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You received your tasks and duties from Dr. Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. She was my managing director, and she issued us with tasks and orders. She told us what to do and who was to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us you were under work obligation. I believe that was issued by the Crisis Staff, since it is a measure undertaken during emergency situations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I didn't use the right term. I was tasked by Dr. Bosanac to manage those 30 people. We were all under an obligation to work. No one could stay at the hospital and do nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether the Crisis Staff of the medical centre in Vukovar ever issued an order in June or July of 1991 concerning the nuclear shelter and its use, as well as storing a significant quantity of medication and medical equipment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that at the time you headed the group you mentioned. Were you given that task immediately upon your return in August, or did you continue with your previous duties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In August one could no longer supply or procure anything because the shelling had already started. So I was tasked with other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I was to tell you that the plane bombings and the shellings on Vukovar began on the 25th of August of 1991 as confirmed by several witnesses, would you say that I'm correct in claiming that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You may be. A lot of time has passed and I can't remember the exact date, but more or less it is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After that date you went to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, if you know, how the Mitnica defence was organised prior to that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that. As I said, I didn't deal with such matters. I never bothered because I was employed at the hospital. But I did go home every day from hospital for as long as I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the group you headed. You said they were men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, only men.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could move into private session, since I intend to ask about the group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We're back in open session, sir. Sir, during combat operations in Vukovar, was there a special service or a unit that had the duty of bringing the wounded and the injured back from the town to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had our own emergency unit and they would bring in the wounded if there was a call to say that somebody had been hurt. Furthermore, there were check-points manned by our Croatian defenders, and whenever one of them was wounded or seriously injured, they would bring these wounded persons back to the hospital in their own vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did they have some sort of radio communication with the duty doctor back at the hospital or the head of the emergency unit, so if there were any calls when anyone got injured they could go out and pick those people up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say they did or if they didn't, but I don't think there was any line of communication open between them. Sometimes they did it on their own initiatives. Sometimes they would pick up a patient at one of the check-points and they would ask us. For example, I personally once gave them one of my vehicles to use because one of their vehicles had been damaged during these transports, and they probably made applications with other people too. But most often, they would bring the wounded in from the check-points to the hospital themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in September 1991 the hospital was still receiving regular medical supplies from other parts of Croatia, from hospitals in other parts of Croatia, by land or by air. There was a helicopter bringing supplies landing at an airfield near the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in October two convoys were organised by the Medecins sans Frontieres. First of all, tell me if you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about the convoy on the 13th of October? Isn't it the fact that they did not get past the barracks because there had been no agreement with the Vukovar command to have the defence lines opened and that's why the convoy got stuck right there? Wasn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, all the convoys were eventually successful. They all left Vukovar eventually and no one ever returned. I may be wrong on that one, but I don't think any of the convoys ever got stuck, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But what about one particular convoy that took a large number of wounded away from the hospital? This was on the 17th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about all the convoys. At least as far as I know. We all knew what was going on in the hospital, me in particular. I was working with those 30 people and then I was assigned to a different job, but I still kept my close cooperation with the hospital's Crisis Staff throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that you cooperated or worked closely together with the Crisis Staff, do you know if the hospital's Crisis Staff at any time received any instructions from the Crisis Staff of Vukovar's defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was cooperation between the two. There was some sort of cooperation, but I never personally witnessed any conversations between them. But I did go there a number of times and I think they did work together, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about this other convoy on the 17th of October, the convoy that arrived at the Vukovar Hospital? Was it escorted by members of the National Guards Corps all the way to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know who decided which persons would join the convoy in order to leave Vukovar and go back to Croatia? Who was in charge of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose it must have been the head nurse, Binazija Kolesar, and Dr. Bosanac herself, as well as Dr. Njavro, who was the chief surgeon. And Dr. Ivica Matos, a urologist, who also performed surgery during the war, as well as Dr. Aleksijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Dr. Matos was a member of the Crisis Staff of Vukovar's defence wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, I can't say. I know that he was a member of the hospital's own Crisis Staff. As for his membership in the other Crisis Staff, the Crisis Staff of Vukovar's defence, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of fact that a wounded soldier by the name of Ivan Zivkovic was taken away from Vukovar on that convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I don't know about a single patient, I think. There was one that I knew of, Darko Dombaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that you saw armed members of the National Guards Corps standing outside in the hospital's courtyard. But did you see them anywhere around the hospital, across the street or near the MUP building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no way I could see them because I never left the hospital compound throughout. My job was within the hospital compound and I hardly ever left the hospital compound throughout those three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know about JNA soldiers being treated at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw those myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: They were in a separate room, a special room and they were being guarded, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about them being guarded or being in some sort of a special room. They were together with all the other patients. All I know is that they were exceptionally scared because we Croats were all branded as Ustashas by the Serbs and people were saying that we were slitting their children's throats. I know that they were treated well, in a fair manner, and I know that what they eventually said is that if they had a say in it, they would have chosen to stay right there and not go anywhere. However, your own people took them back.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ever go to those rooms where these JNA soldiers were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And you say that you never saw any security detail outside their rooms, no one standing guard, the rooms where the patients were, or next to their beds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the way I remember it, but I can't be certain about this, it's been 15 years, after all, and it wasn't something important that I was watching out for. But I don't think there was any security detail assigned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
